detail.scope: Commercial-sector electricity sales and average price by state, as reported to EIA. Data centers are billed mostly in the commercial class, so this is a proxy for their load, not a measurement of it.

sources.name: ERCOT
sources.scope: Large generators with a full interconnection study requested, from the monthly Generator Interconnection Status report for Texas. Includes projects from study through commissioning.

sources.name: NYISO
sources.scope: Projects in the New York interconnection queue as NYISO publishes them.

sources.scope: Projects in the Midcontinent generator interconnection queue, all statuses as MISO publishes them.

sources.scope: Generator interconnection requests across the south-central US, all statuses as SPP publishes them, withdrawn requests counted separately.

sources.name: CAISO
sources.scope: Active generator interconnection requests on the California ISO grid, from the public queue report. Completed and withdrawn projects are counted separately.

analysis.body:
As of mid-September 2026, the eight states tracked by EIA commercial electricity sales show 54.8 terawatt-hours consumed in the prior quarter at an average price of $14.20 per megawatt-hour, with California commanding the highest rate at $27.33/MWh and Texas the lowest at $8.66/MWh. These commercial-sector numbers serve as a proxy for data center load since hyperscale facilities are billed primarily in this class, though they do not isolate data center consumption from other commercial users. Texas leads absolute consumption with 15.75 TWh, followed by California at 10.02 TWh and Virginia at 7.77 TWh, the latter two reflecting significant existing data center footprints.

Across the five major grid interconnection queues, 8,378 projects totaling 1.33 terawatts of planned generation and storage capacity await connection, with ERCOT's Texas queue alone representing 438 GW. Gas represents 184.5 GW of this queue demand (13.9 percent), while storage—the category most responsive to the irregular power draw of AI workloads—accounts for 327.6 GW (24.7 percent). Solar, at 228.9 GW, dominates the fuel mix, underscoring the industry-wide build-out of renewable capacity in regions where data centers are clustering. The sheer scale of queued resources suggests interconnection timelines and grid upgrades will remain critical constraints through 2027 and beyond.

Storage growth in particular tracks data center expansion patterns: SPP's south-central queue holds 52.9 GW of storage against 42.2 GW of wind, ERCOT's has 159.8 GW against 48.2 GW of wind, and CAISO's holds 46.9 GW against just 4.6 GW of wind. This storage-heavy profile reflects the need to smooth out high-frequency demand spikes and diurnal solar variability that AI compute clusters create. Watch for quarterly updates to queue withdrawal rates and study-to-construction timelines, as delays in storage interconnection could emerge as the primary bottleneck for data center capacity additions.
